lessonTitle: Structured Clinical Examination Skills: Assessed Performance

blocks.text: The bell rings and you have eight minutes with an actor playing a 62-year-old man who 'gets out of breath'. Candidates who start examining before introducing themselves lose marks they could never have recovered; candidates who ask 40 questions and run out of time never examine at all. A structured clinical examination rewards a plan, not just knowledge.

blocks.markdown: **What the examination tests.** An objective structured clinical examination (OSCE) uses a series of timed stations, each assessing defined skills against a mark scheme: history taking, examination, interpretation of data, communication, procedures and professionalism. The examiner scores observable behaviours, so what you say and do must be visible. Preparation consists of a repeatable structure for each type of station, practised against the clock.

rows: Identify the task, the patient, the time and any instruction such as 'examine only the chest'
Wash hands, introduce yourself, confirm name and date of birth, explain and gain consent, check comfort and pain
Follow a rehearsed structure: key symptom characteristics, relevant risks, red flags; or inspect, palpate, percuss, auscultate
Efficient coverage of what the stem asks
Thank the patient, cover them, wash hands, summarise to the patient or examiner
Courtesy and a clear take-home message
Give a concise summary, the leading diagnosis and a differential, and suggest next investigations
blocks.caption: A generic station structure. Adapt to the task; never skip introduction, consent and hand hygiene.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: budgeting time in an 8-minute history and examination station
blocks.prompt: The stem reads: 'Mr N, 62, gets breathless on exertion. Take a focused history (about 4 minutes), examine the respiratory system (about 3 minutes) and tell the examiner your impression.' Plan the station.

steps.text: Allocate the time: 30 seconds opening, 3.5 minutes of history, 3 minutes of examination, 1 minute for closing and an impression. Check the clock at fixed points.

History focus: onset and progression of breathlessness, exercise tolerance in a concrete measure (for example stairs or flat distance), cough, sputum and haemoptysis, wheeze, chest pain, orthopnoea and oedema, smoking and occupational exposures, relevant background and medicines. Use open questions first, then closed questions that separate respiratory from cardiac causes.

Examination: observe from the end of the bed (respiratory rate, work of breathing, cyanosis), hands (clubbing, tar staining, tremor), pulse and JVP, then the chest: inspect, palpate expansion, percuss and auscultate front and back. Offer to complete with peak flow or spirometry, oxygen saturations and a chest X-ray.

Close and summarise: cover the patient, thank him and tell the examiner 'This is a 62-year-old smoker with progressive exertional breathlessness. I think COPD is most likely; I would also consider heart failure and interstitial lung disease, and I would request spirometry and a chest X-ray.'

blocks.answer: A timed structure of opening, history, examination and a clear closing impression gives full coverage without running out of time.

blocks.markdown: **Interpreting common results.** Stations often hand you a result and ask what it means. Use the pattern: confirm it belongs to this patient, compare with the reference interval (which varies by laboratory), check the units, then say what it suggests and what you would do next.

rows: Iron deficiency, chronic blood loss or thalassaemia trait
Ferritin, iron studies, look for the source of blood loss
Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol, thyroid or liver disease
B12, folate, thyroid and liver tests, alcohol history
Raised TSH with low free T4
Treat with thyroid hormone replacement; check doses against BNF
Consistent with diabetes (confirm if no symptoms)
Repeat or confirm, assess for complications
Airflow obstruction (for example COPD or asthma)
blocks.caption: Reference ranges and thresholds vary by laboratory and guideline; confirm against the local range and current NICE guidance.

FEV1 is the volume exhaled in the first second of a forced breath; FVC is the total volume exhaled. A fixed ratio of 0.70 is widely used to define obstruction; some guidelines use the lower limit of normal.
ARR is the absolute risk reduction; NNT is the number needed to treat to prevent one event over the stated period. Both are easier for patients to understand than relative changes.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: explaining a result to a patient
blocks.prompt: Mrs P, 45, has had tiredness and weight gain. Her blood tests show a raised TSH and a low free T4. Explain the result to her in an OSCE station. Also, if a treatment reduces the 5-year risk of an event from 10% to 7%, how would you express the benefit?

steps.text: Open: check what she knows ('What have you been told about your blood tests?') and how much she wants to know. Warn her that you will give some information: 'The tests have shown something that explains why you feel tired.'

Explain in plain language, in short chunks: 'The thyroid is a small gland in your neck that sets the speed of the body. Your tests show it is underactive. That can cause tiredness, weight gain and feeling cold. It is common and treatable with a daily tablet.' Avoid jargon; if you use a term, explain it. State that the dose is tailored and monitored by blood tests (doses are for the prescriber and must be checked against BNF).

Check understanding with teach-back ('Just so I know I explained it clearly, could you tell me in your own words what we found?'), invite questions, address concerns and agree the next step (a prescription and a repeat blood test in a set time).

For the risk statement, use natural frequencies: 'Out of 100 people like you, about 10 would have the event over 5 years without treatment and about 7 with treatment, so treatment prevents the event in about 3 of every 100 people.' The absolute risk reduction is 0.10 minus 0.07, which is 0.03, and the number needed to treat is 1 / 0.03, about 33.

blocks.answer: Explain the thyroid result in plain chunks with a check for understanding, and express treatment benefit as an absolute change (3 fewer events per 100, NNT about 33) rather than as a relative percentage.

blocks.markdown: **Breaking down communication.** Good explanation uses open questions, silence, signposting ('I'd like to talk about two things'), chunk-and-check, plain language, and an invitation to ask questions. For serious news a staged approach such as SPIKES (Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, Strategy and summary) can help. Respond to emotion before adding information.

**Learning from feedback.** The station is a learning event. Reflective models such as Gibbs' cycle or the 'What? So what? Now what?' model structure the process: describe what happened, analyse why, and decide on a specific action. A useful goal is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound (SMART). Seek specific examples from the examiner or peer, practise the weak skill deliberately with feedback, and re-test. Keep reflection professional: no patient identifiers and no blame.

blocks.title: Common errors in stations
blocks.text: Do not forget hand hygiene or consent. Do not give a diagnosis as certain when the information is limited. Never invent examination findings that were not offered; say that you would examine, then report only what the actor or examiner provides. Do not quote doses or regimens unless you can verify them in the BNF and local guidance.

items: Rehearse a fixed structure for each common type of station and time it.
Use plain language and teach-back whenever you explain.
Express risks as natural frequencies and absolute numbers.
After feedback, write a specific action and review it within a fixed time.

points: An OSCE rewards a visible, timed structure: read the stem, open professionally, focus, close and summarise.
Interpret results by confirming identity, comparing with the reference range, naming the pattern and the next step; thresholds vary by laboratory and guideline.
Explain results in plain chunks with teach-back, and give benefit as an absolute risk change.
Reflect on feedback with a model such as 'What? So what? Now what?', set a SMART goal and re-test the skill.

questions.stem: You enter an examination station and the stem asks you to take a history from a patient with a rash. What should you do first?

options.text: Wash your hands, introduce yourself, confirm the patient's name and date of birth, and explain the purpose and gain consent
Start with the examination to save time
Ask about the patient's family history of rashes
Present the likely diagnosis to the examiner

questions.correctOptionText: Wash your hands, introduce yourself, confirm the patient's name and date of birth, and explain the purpose and gain consent

distractorRationale.a: Correct: introduction, identity check and consent are the first behaviours in every station.
distractorRationale.b: Examining before establishing consent breaches professional practice.
distractorRationale.c: Family history is relevant later, but not before the opening.
distractorRationale.d: A diagnosis cannot be given before taking the history.

questions.explanation: Every station begins with hand hygiene, introduction, identity confirmation and consent. These behaviours are assessed in their own right and underpin trust and safety.

questions.stem: With two minutes left in a history station you have not asked about red-flag symptoms, but you still have a long list of routine systems-review questions. What is the best action?

options.text: Ask the key red-flag and discriminating questions for the presenting complaint, then summarise to the patient
Complete the whole systems review in order
Stop talking and examine silently
Ask the patient to repeat the story

questions.correctOptionText: Ask the key red-flag and discriminating questions for the presenting complaint, then summarise to the patient

distractorRationale.a: Correct: prioritise the questions that rank dangerous and likely diagnoses, then close with a summary.
distractorRationale.b: The systems review is lower priority and will consume the time.

questions.explanation: Time management in a station means prioritising the items that distinguish dangerous from benign causes. A brief summary at the end shows structure and checks accuracy.

questions.stem: You have 8 minutes with a 55-year-old man who has had 30 minutes of central chest pain. Describe how you would structure a focused history and brief examination, including time allocation and what you would say at the end.
markingGuide: Read the stem, wash hands, introduce, confirm identity, explain and gain consent (about 30 seconds)
Focused history with a structure such as site, onset, character, radiation, associated symptoms, timing, exacerbating or relieving factors and severity, plus breathlessness, sweating, syncope
Risk factors and background: smoking, hypertension, diabetes, lipids, family history, previous cardiac disease, medicines; red flags for pulmonary embolism and aortic dissection
Focused examination: general appearance and observations, pulse, blood pressure in both arms if dissection is suspected, heart sounds, chest, calves, and an offer of ECG and troponin
Close: cover and thank the patient, summarise findings to the patient or examiner with a leading diagnosis (for example acute coronary syndrome) and a differential, and state the next investigations
Time checks: about 4 minutes history, 2 minutes examination, remainder for the close
questions.explanation: A good answer keeps to time, covers the discriminating features of chest pain and includes the dangerous alternatives. Marks are lost for omitting consent or for failing to give a differential.

questions.stem: A spirometry report gives FEV1 2.1 L and FVC 3.5 L. Calculate the FEV1/FVC ratio (as a decimal to two places).
questions.explanation: Ratio = 2.1 / 3.5 = 0.60. A ratio below 0.70 supports airflow obstruction, so the finding fits COPD or asthma in the correct clinical context. Interpret alongside symptoms, smoking history and reversibility testing, and check the local reference approach.

questions.stem: A drug reduces the 5-year risk of a stroke from 8 in 100 to 6 in 100 in a trial. Calculate the number needed to treat to prevent one stroke over 5 years.
questions.explanation: Absolute risk reduction = 0.08 - 0.06 = 0.02, so NNT = 1 / 0.02 = 50. About 50 patients must be treated for 5 years to prevent one stroke, a fact more understandable to a patient than a relative reduction of 25%.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with heavy periods and tiredness has a haemoglobin of 92 g/L with a low MCV of 68 fL. Which interpretation is most likely?

options.text: Microcytic anaemia consistent with iron deficiency from menstrual blood loss
Macrocytic anaemia from vitamin B12 deficiency
Normal blood count
Polycythaemia

questions.correctOptionText: Microcytic anaemia consistent with iron deficiency from menstrual blood loss

distractorRationale.a: Correct: low haemoglobin with a low MCV and heavy menstrual loss is the classic pattern of iron deficiency.
distractorRationale.b: B12 deficiency gives a raised MCV.
distractorRationale.c: A haemoglobin of 92 g/L is below the usual female reference interval.

questions.explanation: A low MCV with anaemia indicates impaired haemoglobin synthesis, most often iron deficiency. The history of heavy menstrual bleeding provides the likely source, and the next step is ferritin and treatment of the cause; reference ranges vary by laboratory.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic man's HbA1c is 62 mmol/mol (the commonly used diagnostic threshold for diabetes is 48 mmol/mol). Which explanation to the patient is best?

options.text: 'This test shows your average blood sugar over the last two to three months is higher than normal and is in the range we see in diabetes. Because you have no symptoms we usually repeat the test to be sure. What questions do you have?'
'Your HbA1c is 62 so you have glycaemic dysregulation consistent with T2DM.'
'Don't worry, it's nothing.'
'You will definitely need insulin injections from now on.'

questions.correctOptionText: 'This test shows your average blood sugar over the last two to three months is higher than normal and is in the range we see in diabetes. Because you have no symptoms we usually repeat the test to be sure. What questions do you have?'

distractorRationale.a: Correct: plain language, accurate meaning of the test, honest about confirmation and an invitation to ask.
distractorRationale.b: Uses jargon and does not check understanding.
distractorRationale.c: False reassurance, ignoring a clearly abnormal result.
distractorRationale.d: Unfounded and frightening; treatment is not decided at this stage.

questions.explanation: Effective explanation uses plain terms, links the number to its meaning and the next step, and invites questions. Diagnostic confirmation and treatment decisions should follow current NICE guidance.

questions.stem: A reflective account of an assessed station is complete once it describes what happened, without needing a specific plan for future learning.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Reflection should move from description to analysis to a concrete action. Without a plan, the learning cycle is not closed.

questions.stem: After a station, the examiner's feedback says your history was disorganised and jumped between topics. Which response is best?

options.text: Ask for a specific example, choose a structured template for the history, practise it in timed stations with a peer observer, and re-assess after a set time
Decide the examiner was unfair and ignore the comment
Memorise more facts about the disease
Avoid history stations in future

questions.correctOptionText: Ask for a specific example, choose a structured template for the history, practise it in timed stations with a peer observer, and re-assess after a set time

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a specific, measurable and time-bound plan tackles the identified weakness.
distractorRationale.c: The comment concerns structure, not factual knowledge.

questions.explanation: Using feedback means identifying the specific problem, selecting a targeted strategy and checking progress. This is the 'now what' step of reflective practice and is more effective than passive review.

questions.stem: You failed a communication station in which you had to explain a new diagnosis. The feedback said you used jargon, did not check understanding and did not respond to the actor's emotional cues. Write a short reflective account using the model 'What? So what? Now what?', including two SMART goals.
markingGuide: What: factual, concise description of the station and the feedback, without patient identifiers or blame
So what: analysis of why (nerves, rehearsed lines, focus on content rather than on the person) and the impact on the patient's understanding and trust; link to professional standards
Now what: specific actions such as practising plain-language explanations, using teach-back and chunk-and-check, and naming and acknowledging emotion
Two SMART goals, for example performing a teach-back in every practice consultation for the next two weeks, and recording one practice explanation each week for peer review
Review: plan when and how progress will be measured, and seek further feedback
Shows honest self-appraisal, a commitment to improvement and confidentiality
questions.explanation: A good reflection moves beyond description to analysis and a measurable plan. It must be honest, specific and professional.
